senses.gloss:
nitya
(‘that which exists always’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘nitya’ is generally used in the Hindu scriptures, in two senses: what is eternal; daily.
That which is beyond time, space and causation, and hence unaffected by them is called ‘nitya’. Only the आत्मन् (the Self or the सोउल्) and ब्रह्मन् (the Absolute or God) fit in with this definition.
In some of the darśanas (philosophies), some other objects like paramāṇus (atoms) or kāla (time) or प्रधान or प्रकृति (Nature, matrix of all insentient objects comprising the three guṇas, सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्) are also considered as नित्य or eternal.
As applied to karmas or prescribed rites, नित्य (or नित्यकर्म) refers to the obligatory duties to be performed daily, such as the सन्ध्या, gāyatrījapa and pañca-महायज्ञस्. They gradually lead to चित्त-शुद्धि or purity of मिन्द्.
Practising any योग should be preceded by the performance of नित्य and naimittika karmas (occasional, but compulsory, rites).

nityasaṁsāri
(‘the eternally transmigra-ting [jīva]’)
------------------------------------------
The द्वैत Vedānta of Madhva (A. D. 1238-1317) categorises the jīvas or individual souls into three groups: मुक्तियोग्यस् (those who are fit for लिबेरतिओन्); नित्य-saṁsārins (the eternally transmigrating ones); and the tamoyogyas (the damned ones).
The nityasaṁāris are sensuous beings who delight only in worldly values and feel no need for ethical or spiritual life. Hence they are forced to transmigrate eternally (nitya = eternally).

Nītiśataka
(‘hundred axioms of good conduct’)
------------------------------------------
Subhāṣitas or Sūktis are a special class of Sanskrit literature (See SŪKTI-SĀHITYA under SANSKRIT LITERATURE.). They comprise the quintessence of human experience gathered over several centuries. The Nītiśataka of भर्तृहरि (circa 100 B. C.) is one such work which is extremely popular even now. The legend goes that he was the king of उज्जयिनी. Being disgusted with the infidelity of his queen, he abdicated the throne in favour of his younger brother विक्रमादित्य (the founder of the Vikramaśaka or the Saṁvat era) and became a mendicant.
The work consists of 101 verses in different metres, divided into ten paddhatis or topics.
A brief summary of the same may now be attempted here:
1. Mūrkhapaddhati— ‘On Fools’ (verses 3-11)
This section deals with wiseacres who are actually fools. It is impossible to convince them since they feel they know everything. In the company of the wise ones they are astute enough to keep mum so that their इग्नोरन्चे is not revealed. Yet, they behave shamelessly before others, and ultimately degrade themselves to the lowest levels.
2. Vidvatpaddhati—‘On the Learned’ (verses 12-21)
As opposed to the behaviour of the fools, this section describes the characte-ristics of the learned and the wise. The language and the content of their erudition is an ornament to the king and his kingdom where they live. Hence, the kings should look upon them with great respect and never belittle them. None can take away their ‘wealth’ called knowledge which is their best ornament. In fact it is विद्या or knowledge that helps a person under all circumstances.
These wise ones know how to behave with different types of persons and keep up their own dignity. People who come into contact with them become learned, truthful and righteous.
3. Mānaśauryapaddhati—‘On Self-respect and Grit’ (verses 22-31)
Men of great self-respect and grit are like lions. A lion even when old and in a decrepit state will never stoop to eating grass to sustain itself but will rather try to attack an elephant. Similarly these heroic men of great self esteem will never demean themselves even in times of dire calamities. And, they will never tolerate enemies who try to dishonour or destroy them.
4. Arthapaddhati—‘On Wealth’ (verses 32-41)
Throughout the ages, a man of practical wisdom and common-sense has realised the importance of money or wealth in one’s personal and social life. This is now being described in a language that is both elegant and humorous. When a person has enough money, none of the qualities that normally make him respectable in the eyes of the public—like high caste, noble virtues, pedigree, or heroism—is necessary. People praise him as a handsome man, as a man of learning, as virtuous and as an orator. This shows that all good qualities are ultimately rooted in money!
The author advises rich persons to enjoy their wealth as also distribute it among the needy ones. Otherwise robbers may take it away!
5. Durjanapaddhati—“On the Wicked” (verses 42-51)
This section describes the nature of positively evil persons, especially the kings and hence how difficult it is to serve them.
The evil qualities normally seen in such persons are: cruelty, pugnacity, greed for others’ wealth, lack of sexual मोरलित्य्, jealousy and so on.
Even if an evil person is endowed with learning or scholarship, he has to be avoided like a poisonous snake.
It has become a habit for them to find fault with good people and to criticise even their good qualities by distorting them.
Kings by nature, because of their position and power, are short-tempered. Hence good persons have to be extremely careful in dealing with them.
Friendship with the evil ones is like the morning shadow, long in the beginning and short later on, totally disappearing by midday. Therefore it should be avoided.
6. Sajjanapaddhati—“On the Virtuous” (verses 52-61)
This part of the book gives a long list of the several virtues or good qualities that go to make a man really great. Some of these are: friendship with the virtuous; humility before the elders and respected persons; devotion to God; self-control; keeping away from the wicked; courage in facing difficulties; heroism in war; great interest in the acquisition of knowledge, especially of the scriptures; liberality in giving gifts; absence of cruelty; decent behaviour towards women; compassion towards the animals; expertise in the performance of one’s duties; absence of boasting about oneself; humility even when he becomes rich; praising the virtues of others; ever eager to help others.
7. Paropakārapaddhati—“On helping others” (verses 62-71)
It is the very nature of great people to do good to others. They are ever eager to do so. Trees bending low while laden with fruits, rain-bearing clouds descending to the earth, sun and मोओन् making the red and blue lotuses to bloom—these natural phenomena have a lot to teach us.
Good people are ever eager to help others, never caring for themselves whereas the evil ones go out of the way to harm others though they have nothing to gain.
Incidentally, the poet gives a beautiful description of a true friend. He prevents you from committing sins, engages you in good actions, protects your secrets, praises your virtues and never forsakes you when you are in difficulties.
8. Dhairyapaddhati—“On Courage” (verses 72-81)
The main theme of this part of the treatise is that men of mettle will never give up an undertaking in the middle but will see through it till the end.
Afraid of the obstacles that may arise, some people never start any work. There are others who may start one but give it up in the middle once they meet with obstacles. But the real heroes are they who will undauntedly accomplish the task they take up in spite of being beset with innumerable obstacles.
Another speciality of these people is that they never swerve from the path of righteousness. They are above all temptations.
9. Daivapaddhati—“On the Power of Fate” (verses 82-91)
In this section of the work, the author forcefully argues, with the help of appropriate examples, that दैव or fate is all- powerful in one’s life and that pauruṣa or human effort is useless! Perhaps the bitter experiences of his own life are being reflected in these verses.
The following are some of the instances to the point: इन्द्र and the gods of हेअवेन् though endowed with all facilities, help and advantages, were frequently defeated and driven out by the दानवस् or demons. Even the best of men created by ब्रह्मा for the good of the world die one day making his efforts null and void.
The death of a mouse that is seeking ड़ोओद्, by falling into the mouth of a hungry snake or of a bald-headed person seeking shelter under a tree being killed by a falling object are other examples.
While advising people to surrender to विधि or fate, he also admires the grit of great people who will never give up in spite of problems and difficulties created by fate!
10. Karmapaddhati—“On the Power of Karma” (verses 92-101)
Though विधि (or ब्रह्मा) is very powerful, even he has to act according to the karmaniyama or the theory of कर्म, ‘As you sow, so you reap’. In this last section the poet advises all to perform good actions and avoid evil ones.
The language of the Śataka is compa-ratively simple and elegant. Some printed editions contain 108 verses or 110 verses instead of 101. There are two Sanskrit commentaries by Mahābala Kṛṣṇaśāstry and M. R. Kāle.
See BHARTṚHARI.

nīti
(‘that which leads [towards the good]’)
------------------------------------------
In the most general sense, the word ‘nīti’ means ‘morality’ and ‘ethics’. In course of time, it came to be considered as an abbreviation of राजनीति or political science.
The word is also used to indicate any systematised form of thought like Śukra-nīti and Viduranīti.
Dharma, which is a more comprehensive word, includes नीति also.

nityānuvāda
(‘a permanent reiterating statement’)
------------------------------------------
The पूर्वमीमाṁसा system of Hindu philosophy deals with the various modes of interpreting and understanding the Vedic statements. One of them is अर्थवाद. (See ARTHAVĀDA for details.)
One of the three aspects of अर्थवाद is अनुवाद. When a statement reiterates something which has already been known otherwise it is called ‘anuvāda’ (anu = following; वाद = stating or statement). For instance, the statement ‘agnir himasya bheṣajam,’ ‘Fire is the antidote for cold’ (Taittirīya Saṁhitā 7.4.18.2) contains a truth already known through direct experience.
A subsidiary aspect of अनुवाद is नित्यानुवाद. When a Vedic text apparently prohibits something which can never happen, it is called ‘nityānuvāda’. For example: ‘The Vedic altar should not be piled on bare earth, nor in the sky, nor in हेअवेन्.’ In this sentence, the piling of the Vedic altar in the way described is never done. The latter two options can never happen! Hence it is called ‘nityānuvāda’.
This word occurs in the Āpastamba Dharmasūtras (2.6.14.3) and in the Pūrva-mīmāṁsāsūtras of जैमिनि (2.4.26; 9.4.36).

nityamukta
(‘the eternally free’)
------------------------------------------
The Vedānta philosophy has branched off into three main schools: advaita, viśiṣṭādvaita and द्वैत.
In the Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta, the jīvas (individual souls) are divided into three varieties of whom nityasūris or nityamuktas (like आदिशेष, गरुड and विष्वक्सेन) are the first. They were never in bondage, but ever happy in the company of Lord विष्णु.
In the द्वैत Vedānta, the word is applied only to ब्रह्मन् or God and लक्ष्मी, his consort.
See VIŚIṢṬĀDVAITA-VEDĀNTA-DARŚANA.

nityalīlā
(‘eternal sport’)
------------------------------------------
Vallabhācārya (A. D. 1473-1531) was an important teacher of the schools of Vedānta that teach, nay, lay great emphasis on भक्ति or devotion to God, as the sole means of God-realisation and लिबेरतिओन्.
He classifies the souls into three types: pravāha (those who are ever busy with worldly life); maryādā (those who follow the Vedic path strictly); and puṣṭi (those who worship the Lord out of pure love engendered only through divine grace).
God, out of his own free will, brings out a puṣṭi-type of सोउल् out of himself, gives him a divine body like his own and sports with him (the puṣṭi-सोउल्) for all time! This divine play is called ‘nityalīlā’ wherein God remains subservient to that सोउल्, giving him the joy of his own company. This joy has been technically called, ‘bhajanānanda’.

Nītiśāstra
(‘the science of moral values or एथिच्स्’)
------------------------------------------
Since नीति (moral values, code of conduct) had always been treated as a part and parcel of धर्म (righteousness) and दर्शन (philosophical system), it has never been construed or presented as an independent branch of knowledge.
Though every दर्शन has prescribed its own modes of spiritual practice, the नीति-part of it is almost the same. The ten सामान्य-dharmas or the first two steps (yama and नियम) of the aṣṭāṅgayoga of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) can epitomise the नीतिशास्त्र.
See also DHARMA and NĪTI.
